newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH PARTIES SQUABBLE AS VOTERS OPT TO STAY AWAY.
newsitem.headline: CZECH PARTIES SQUABBLE AS VOTERS OPT TO STAY AWAY.

text.p: As Czechs prepare for Senate election run-offs, the ruling coalition and opposition Social Democrats are both so consumed by infighting that many voters believe the only way of registering a protest is to stay away.
Turnout in last weekend's first round of the polls was 35 percent and if the reason was public disgust with politicians, the run-off on Friday and Saturday may be no better.
Voter apathy has made a mockery of predictions that the elections to the new upper house could indicate the future of conservative Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's minority government.
Between the rounds, the two sides have burnt as much energy on internal bickering as on attacking their opponents.

Klaus has exchanged insults with his junior coalition partners over mutual support, or the lack of it, in the run-offs, while leading Social Democrats have blamed each other over their poor first round performance.

In last weekend's first round, only four candidates gained the necessary majority of votes to clinch their constituency. In the remaining 77 constituencies, the first round winner and runner-up will contest the run-off.
In 47 constituencies, the run-off is a straight fight between the two biggest parties, Klaus's centre-right Civic Democratic Party (ODS) and the centre-left Social Democrats.
But in a further 24, ODS candidates will face representatives of the two junior coalition partners, the Christian Democrats and the Civic Democratic Alliance (ODA).
Relations have long been strained in the coalition and got no better when it lost its lower house majority in June.

Tempers snapped a week before the first round when Christian Democrat leader Josef Lux alleged that the state intelligence agency, led by a Klaus protege, had spied on him and then doctored its reports to conceal the operation.

Klaus sacrificed the agency's acting director but this week he has engaged Lux in a public slanging match. Lux, concerned that the ODS might dominate the Senate due to its first past the post voting system, has said his party would back the ODS in only some of the run-offs and Social Democrats in others.
Klaus bitterly attacked a failure by Lux and ODA leader Jan Kalvoda to offer blanket support for ODS in the second round.

"I ... regard it as scandalous that we did not manage to find a common voice which would say to voters... that even though we have different views on minor issues, our opinion on the future of this Senate is the same," he said.

Lux blasted Klaus for phoning candidates from the junior partners who failed to make it to the run-off, asking them to endorse the ODS in the second round. "When the prime minister has made a mistake he should admit it and correct it," he said.
No one is saying the coalition will split, but Christian Democrat policies lie closest to those of the Social Democrats, whose leader Milos Zeman has long tried to woo Lux.
ODS won a strong 36.5 percent of the first round vote and Lux has expressed fears that it may dominate the Senate.
But things look no better with the Social Democrats, who won only 20.3 percent of the first round vote.
Deputy chairman Karel Machovec accused Zeman of adopting too confrontational a tone during campaigning and of defying party policy by negotiating with the unreformed Communists.
At a Social Democrat rally in the western town of Rokycany, some voters still gave Zeman the benefit of the doubt.

"I used to trust ODS at the beginning but now I see that they only care about themselves," said a 68-year-old retired woman. "We need somebody with clean hands and genuine interest in people, and that is Zeman."

But one woman was sick of them all. "I just stopped here on the way home because my kids wanted to see somebody who they only know from the telly," she said. "I'm not going to vote, because it's pointless. They are all the same as each other."
-- Prague newsroom (42 2) 24 23 0003
